Along both edges run rows of stiff, hairlike papillae. These are not whiskers in the ordinary sense. Each one is a pressure organ and a chemical tongue at once. When the vell moves, the papillae brush stone, pooled condensate, and the faint thermal plumes that rise from cracks in the crust. It builds a map from touch the way other animals build one from sight.

Its “head” is only the end that usually leads. There is a mouth—a soft, muscular slit—and around it a ring of deeper pits that taste dissolved minerals and the waste gases of the microbial mats it feeds on. It does not hunt in bursts. It grazes. The mats grow where warm water seeps through rock, and the vell follows those seeps by the taste of sulfur and metal ions, and by the slight warmth against its underside.

Locomotion is a slow lateral wave. It has no limbs. Rings of muscle tighten and release, and tiny hooked scales on the belly catch the rock so it does not slide backward. In open caverns it can swim, poorly, by the same wave, through pools so still that a dropped pebble would be an event. It prefers walls and floors. Open water is a place where it can be found.

Hearing, for a vell, is the whole body. The skin is stretched over fluid-filled channels that pick up low vibrations: the tick of contracting rock, the drip of condensate, the heavier, rhythmic thump of something larger moving three chambers away. It has no ears and no echolocation clicks. Sound is passive. It listens by lying still and letting the cave speak through its ribs.

What passes for a brain is a long cord with thickenings, not a single knot. Memory is spatial and chemical. A vell that has crossed a gallery once can cross it again in the dark—not by pictures, but by the sequence of textures, temperatures, and tastes, the way a person might retrace a path by the feel of doorframes and the smell of kitchens. Individuals leave faint mucus trails laced with a signature mixture of salts. Others read them. Territories are not seen boundaries. They are flavors that say *this stone has already been claimed, and recently*.

It has no eyes, no pigment, no display colors, no light of its own. Communication is contact and chemistry: a brief press of flanks, a change in the mucus, a patterned tremor sent through the rock with the belly scales. Mating is a slow alignment in a warm seep, two ribbons matching their waves until the chemistries agree. The vell’s gait is deliberate: three pads always planted, body low, head sweeping side to side so the chemoreceptors sample a wide arc.

When it must cross open ground, it drums. A hardened plate under the throat taps the rock in short patterns. Echoes return through the lateral lines. The resolution is crude—boulder, hollow, drop, living mass—but enough to keep it from walking off a shelf.

The vell grazes these mats and also hunts the small, wormlike animals that graze them more efficiently. Its mouth is a circular, muscular ring lined with backward-facing keratin hooks. Electric fields matter. Many of Nerath’s small animals generate weak bioelectric pulses as they move through conductive brine. Lost vells walk in widening spirals until the magnetic feeling and a familiar chemical front coincide.

Conflict is mostly display. A threatened vell inflates its flank sacs and releases a bitter aerosol. The rival reads the concentration and either yields or answers with a stronger plume. It will never know that other worlds have light. It does not miss it. On Nerath, light would be a useless extra, and eyes would be soft tissue waiting to freeze. The vell is not incomplete. It is built exactly for the planet it has.

Skin is not skin but a mat of mineral-laced fibers that stiffen or soften with temperature. In the coldest reaches it goes rigid as wire; nearer a vent it becomes slick and almost liquid, able to pour itself through a fissure narrower than a finger.

It does not see, hear, or smell in any way we would recognize. The entire surface is a pressure organ. Every grain of grit that brushes it, every faint tremor in the stone, every slight change in the density of the slurry registers as a pattern across that skin. A thrum can tell the difference between a settling pebble and the footfall of another of its kind from several body-lengths away. It navigates by the geometry of vibration the way a bat navigates by echoes, except the “sound” is the planet itself creaking.

Feeding is slow and chemical. Along both edges of the ribbon run rows of pores that weep a weak acid, dissolving trace metals and simple organics locked in the rock. The dissolved slurry is drawn inward through channels no wider than a hair and metabolized by colonies of microbes the thrum carries in internal pockets. Those microbes are as much a part of it as its cartilage. When food is scarce, the thrum slows until its pulse—a sluggish contraction that travels the length of the ribbon once every few hours—nearly stops. It can remain in that near-stillness for years.

Reproduction is a matter of division under stress. If a vent cools or a passage collapses, the ribbon pinches at its middle and the two halves separate. Each half already contains a full set of the microbial partners and enough stored minerals to regrow the missing length. There is no mating, no courtship, no sex. The only social behavior is avoidance: two thrums that meet will each shift their pulse rhythm until the interference pattern tells them which way the other is moving, and then they drift apart. Crowding means shared food, and food is already almost nothing.

Color is meaningless here, but if a light were somehow brought to it, the thrum would look dull gray-brown, the color of wet slate, with paler streaks where mineral deposits have crusted along old scars. It would not react to the light. Light is not a stimulus it has any receptor for. It would only notice the heat of the lamp, and it would recoil from that the way we recoil from a burn, folding itself into the coldest shadow it can find until the strange warmth passed.

In the absolute dark it is not lonely and not afraid. It is a slow question the rock asks of itself, answered, over centuries, by a ribbon that listens to stone and eats what the stone is willing to give.

Where a head would be, there is only a shallow, star-shaped mouth surrounded by six soft, retractable palps. Each palp ends in a chemoreceptive pad. It tastes the world the way a moth tastes night air—metals, moisture, the chemical signature of prey, the sour trace of a rival’s trail. Inside the mouth, rows of keratin combs scrape bacterial films and mineral crusts off cave walls. It is not a hunter by default. Most of its calories come from chemosynthetic mats that grow where warm, mineral-rich water seeps from cracks. When those mats fail, it becomes an ambush scavenger: it presses flat against a wall, stills its breath, and waits for something warm to brush its bristles.

Its metabolism is almost idle. A vellum can go weeks between real meals by dropping its body temperature until it matches the rock. Blood is thick and dark, rich in a protein that binds what little oxygen the atmosphere holds and that also carries dissolved metals it needs for enzymes. It does not pant or sweat. Heat is a liability; radiating it would announce it to anything that can sense infrared. So it keeps a narrow thermal shadow, barely warmer than the stone.
